fajr.summary: The dawn prayer — the first of the five daily obligatory prayers.
fajr.why: Allah commanded establishing prayer at the edges of the day; Fajr marks the start of the Muslim day and was never abandoned by the Prophet ﷺ in congregation or alone.
fajr.benefits: Whoever prays Fajr is under Allah's protection. It is witnessed by the angels of the night and day and brings light for the rest of the day.

sunrise.summary: The moment the sun rises above the horizon — a time marker, not a prayer itself.
sunrise.why: Prayer is forbidden while the sun is rising (and at zenith and setting) so the ummah does not resemble sun-worshippers. Knowing sunrise helps time Ishraq and avoid invalid prayer times.
sunrise.benefits: Observing Allah's signs in the sky increases awe (taqwa) and helps structure the morning sunnah prayers correctly.

ishraq.summary: A two-rak'ah sunnah prayer after the sun has fully risen (about 15–20 minutes after sunrise).
ishraq.why: Prophet ﷺ sid whoever prys Fjr په cپهgregtiپه n sits rememberپهg ټولh until sunrدیe, n prys two rk'hs, receives  rewrd د  complete Hjj او 'Umrh.
ishraq.benefits: Immense reward with minimal effort when combined with Fajr in congregation. A peaceful start to the day in zikr and optional prayer.

duha.summary: The forenoon prayer — typically two to eight rak'ahs between sunrise and Dhuhr.
duha.why: Charity is due on every joint of the body each day; even a few rak'ahs of Duha fulfills that charity for the limbs through worship.
duha.benefits: Forgives sins, brings sustenance (rizq), and revives a neglected sunnah. Flexible timing makes it accessible when the day allows.

dhuhr.summary: The midday prayer — the second obligatory prayer, when the sun passes its zenith.
dhuhr.why: The five daily prayers were made obligatory on the Night Journey; Dhuhr breaks the day's busyness with remembrance of Allah.
dhuhr.benefits: The Prophet ﷺ said the first deed judged on the Day of Resurrection is prayer. Guarding Dhuhr protects the rest of one's deeds.

asr.summary: The afternoon prayer — the middle prayer emphasized in the Qur'an.
asr.why: Allah specifically warns about guarding the middle prayer (Salat al-Wusta). It falls when many are busy or tired, so preserving it is a sign of sincerity.
asr.benefits: Whoever mدیses sr, it دی s if he lost hدی fmily او welth — highروښانهپهg its weight. Keepپهg it strengns dدیciplپهe through  dy.

maghrib.summary: The sunset prayer — prayed immediately after the sun has set.
maghrib.why: The time opens right at sunset; delaying without reason risks missing the preferred window. The Prophet ﷺ warned against neglecting prayer until the sun has set.
maghrib.benefits: Marks gratitude at the day's end and was among the first prayers the Prophet ﷺ emphasized to his companions.

isha.summary: The night prayer — the last of the five obligatory prayers, after twilight fades.
isha.why: Completes  cycle د ورځنی wیاship.  Prophet ﷺ sid if someپهe pryed دیh په cپهgregtiپه, it دی s if he pryed hlf  شپه.

witr.summary: An odd-numbered prayer (usually one or three rak'ahs) after Isha before Fajr — sunnah mu'akkadah, not one of the five fard prayers.
witr.why: The Prophet ﷺ said Allah is Witr (One) and loves Witr, so maintain the Witr prayer. He never abandoned it, even when traveling.

travel.title: Travelling & prayer
travel.subtitle: Qasr, Jam', and what the Qur'an and Sunnah teach about salah on a journey
travel.takeaway: Allah legislated shortening (Qasr) and combining (Jam') out of mercy for the traveller — not to abandon prayer, but to ease its performance on the road.
travel.obligationsTitle: Wht تاسو دي still respپهsible لپاره
travel.rakatsNote: Only the fard is shown. Sunnah rawatib and Witr are discussed below — they remain recommended, though many travellers lighten them for hardship.

quran.excerpt: When you travel through the land, there is no blame on you if you shorten the prayer, if you fear that those who disbelieve may harm you. Indeed, the disbelievers are ever a clear enemy to you.

hadith.excerpt: Anas said: We travelled with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. The mu'adhin called for prayer and he said: 'Pray two rakahs' — and he did the same for the other prayers except Maghrib (three) and Fajr (two).

Prophet ﷺ sid: 'ټولh loves هغه Hدی cپهcessiپهs be tken, just s He htes ته be dدیobeyed.'

obligations: The five daily prayers remain obligatory — shortened (Qasr) when you qualify as a traveller.

Each shortened prayer is prayed like the first two rakahs of the full prayer — recite Al-Fatiha and a surah, bow, prostrate, then sit for tashahhud and salam.
When you return home or intend to settle, resume praying each prayer in full at its proper time.
Missed prayers while travelling must still be made up (qaza) — travel does not waive what was omitted.

qasr.title: Qsr — shیاtenپهg
qasr.body: The four-rakah fard prayers — Dhuhr, Asr, and Isha — are prayed as two rakahs on a qualifying journey. Pray them exactly as the first two rakahs at home: standing recitation, one ruku, two sujud, tashahhud, and salam. Fajr stays two rakahs and Maghrib stays three; neither is shortened. Qasr applies to the fard only.

jam.title: Jm' — combپهپهg
jam.body: A traveller may combine Dhuhr with Asr into one sitting, and Maghrib with Isha into one sitting — praying both fard prayers back-to-back with one adhan and iqamah. Fajr cannot be combined with any other prayer. Combining is a separate concession from shortening: you may shorten without combining, combine without shortening (in some situations), or do both together.

jamTypes.title: Jm' l-Tqdim & l-T'khir
jamTypes.body: Jam' al-Taqdim (early combining): pray both prayers together at the earlier prayer's time — e.g. Dhuhr and Asr at Dhuhr time. Jam' al-Ta'khir (delayed combining): pray both at the later prayer's time — e.g. Dhuhr and Asr at Asr time. The Prophet ﷺ combined at Arafah (Dhuhr at Asr time) and at Muzdalifah (Maghrib at Isha time), establishing both forms.

when.title: When cپهcessiپهs begپه & end
when.body: Concessions begin once you leave your town or city on a journey — not for daily commutes within your locality. They end when you return home, or when you intend to stay at your destination for the period scholars define as 'settling' (the number of days differs between schools). If you are unsure whether you still count as a traveller, ask a scholar before assuming the concessions.

sunnah.body: The emphasized sunnah prayers (rawatib) before and after fard remain virtuous but are not required. Many scholars permit leaving them while travelling due to hardship, especially when combining prayers. Hayd is the regular monthly bleeding most women experience at a familiar time each cycle. Scholars discuss a minimum duration (some say one day and night, others require more) and a maximum duration — commonly cited figures range from about 10 to 15 days depending on the school of thought.

Practically, note your usual pattern (‘ada): how many days hayd typically lasts and when it usually begins. Istihada is bleeding outside the normal hayd period — between cycles, after puberty before the first regular period, or when bleeding continues past the maximum hayd duration.

Unlike hayd, istihada does not lift the obligation to pray and fast. A woman with istihada generally performs wudu for each prayer while bleeding is active; the bleeding itself does not invalidate wudu according to many scholars.

Distinguishing hayd from istihada can be difficult. Women with a known cycle often rely on their habit, the time of the month, and the characteristics of the blood. If you are unsure whether bleeding is hayd or istihada, pause obligatory tracking only when you are confident it is hayd, and consult a qualified scholar for your specific case.

positions.body:
The default is to pray standing with full ruku and sujud. If standing causes severe pain, weakness, or harm, pray sitting — many scholars permit sitting even without standing first when illness makes standing genuinely difficult.

If you cannot sit upright, pray lying on your side or back, gesturing for ruku and sujud with your head. Use every position concession before skipping a prayer entirely.

When you cannot perform full bowing, incline your head for ruku — a deeper incline for sujud. This is the concession used when praying sitting or lying down.

If you cannot move your head at all, scholars differ on the minimum movement required — some allow intention alone in extreme cases, while others require whatever movement is physically possible.

If you lose consciousness, fall into deep sleep through a prayer time, or are so severely ill that you cannot pray even with all position concessions — and the entire time for that prayer passes — that prayer is waived with no sin, but must be made up (qaza) when you recover.

Marking a day as excused (illness) in this app pauses obligatory tracking and holds your streak — it does not replace the obligation to make up missed prayers later.

If fasting in Ramadan would worsen your illness or delay recovery, break the fast and make it up on other days after you recover — the Qur'an explicitly permits this for the ill.

Each missed Ramadan fast is made up with one day of fasting later; there is no kaffarah (expiation) unless the fast was broken without a valid excuse.

Missed salah during illness must also be made up in order once you are able — unlike hayd, where missed prayers are not qaza. When you recover, resume normal tracking and work through your qaza at a sustainable pace.

descriptions.newYear: The first of Muharram opens the Hijri (lunar) year, whose count begins from the Prophet's migration (Hijrah) from Makkah to Madinah. Muharram is one of the four sacred months and the Prophet ﷺ called it "the month of Allah," naming its voluntary fasting the best after Ramadan (Sahih Muslim 1163). It is a time to reflect on the year past and renew good intentions. There is no specific mandated ritual for the day itself, so beware of unfounded "New Year" practices; increasing voluntary fasting across the month is the established Sunnah.
descriptions.ashura: The 10th of Muharram. The Prophet ﷺ found the Jews of Madinah fasting it in gratitude for Allah saving Musa and the Children of Israel from Pharaoh, and said, "We have more right to Musa than you," then fasted it and told the Muslims to fast (Sahih al-Bukhari 2004). Fasting Ashura expiates the minor sins of the previous year (Sahih Muslim 1162). To differ from other communities, it is recommended to also fast the 9th (Tasu'a): the Prophet ﷺ intended to do so the following year (Sahih Muslim 1134). Fasting the 9th and 10th together is the preferred practice.
descriptions.mawlid: The 12th of Rabi al-Awwal is widely associated with the birth of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ (the exact date is debated among historians). Muslims universally love and honour him and are commanded to send blessings upon him (Qur'an 33:56). Whether to hold a dedicated annual celebration (Mawlid) is a point on which mainstream scholars differ: many, especially in the Sufi and traditional traditions, permit or encourage gatherings of remembrance and sending salawat, while others (notably in the Salafi tradition) hold that a fixed yearly observance was not practised by the early generations and so should be avoided. This app presents the day neutrally; increasing salawat and following the Prophet's Sunnah are agreed goods.
descriptions.isra: Al-Isra wa al-Mi'raj commemorates the Prophet's ﷺ miraculous Night Journey from Makkah to Jerusalem (al-Aqsa) and his ascension through the heavens, referenced in Qur'an 17:1 and 53. On this night the five daily prayers were prescribed — originally fifty, then reduced to five by Allah's mercy while their reward remained fifty (Sahih al-Bukhari 349). The night affirms the sanctity of al-Aqsa and the centrality of Salah. Its precise date (commonly placed on 27 Rajab) is not firmly established, and no specific worship is authentically tied to the night itself; guarding the five daily prayers is its lasting lesson.
descriptions.ramadan: The ninth month and the fourth pillar of Islam. Fasting from dawn to sunset is obligatory on every capable adult Muslim (Qur'an 2:183–185). It is the month in which the Qur'an was first revealed (Qur'an 2:185). The Prophet ﷺ said, "Whoever fasts Ramadan out of faith and seeking reward will have his past sins forgiven" (Sahih al-Bukhari 38). Nights are enlivened with Taraweeh prayer, and the last ten days carry Laylat al-Qadr. It is a month of fasting, Qur'an, charity, and drawing near to Allah.
descriptions.laylatQadr: The Night of Decree — "better than a thousand months" (Qur'an 97:3), the night the Qur'an began to descend. Worship on it outweighs a lifetime of over eighty-three years. The Prophet ﷺ said, "Whoever stands (in prayer) on Laylat al-Qadr out of faith and seeking reward will have his past sins forgiven" (Sahih al-Bukhari 1901). Its exact night is hidden; seek it in the odd nights of the last ten of Ramadan — the 21st, 23rd, 25th, 27th, and 29th (Sahih al-Bukhari 2017), with the 27th especially hoped for. Spend these nights in prayer, Qur'an, and the dua: "Allahumma innaka 'afuwwun tuhibbu al-'afwa fa'fu 'anni."
descriptions.eidFitr: The Festival of Breaking the Fast, on the 1st of Shawwal, marks the end of Ramadan. The day begins with the Eid prayer and is preceded by Zakat al-Fitr, a charity given before the prayer so the poor may also rejoice. Muslims recite the takbir, wear their best, exchange greetings, and strengthen family and community ties. Fasting is forbidden on this day (Sahih al-Bukhari 1991) — it is a day of gratitude and permitted celebration for the worship completed in Ramadan.
descriptions.arafah: The 9th of Dhul-Hijjah, the greatest day of Hajj, when pilgrims stand in worship on the plain of Arafah — "Hajj is Arafah." It falls within the blessed first ten days of Dhul-Hijjah, days in which righteous deeds are more beloved to Allah than any others (Sahih al-Bukhari 969). For those not on Hajj, fasting this day is highly recommended: it expiates the sins of the previous year and the coming year (Sahih Muslim 1162). Pilgrims themselves do not fast, so as to have strength for the standing and supplication.
descriptions.eidAdha: The Festival of Sacrifice, on the 10th of Dhul-Hijjah, is the greater of the two Eids and coincides with the culmination of Hajj. It commemorates Prophet Ibrahim's willingness to sacrifice his son in obedience to Allah, who ransomed him with a ram (Qur'an 37:100–107). Those able offer a sacrifice (Udhiyah/Qurbani), sharing the meat with family, neighbours, and the poor. The day begins with the Eid prayer and takbir and continues through the three days of Tashriq. Fasting is forbidden on this day and the days of Tashriq (Sahih al-Bukhari 1991).

basics.title: Wht دی zkt?
basics.body:
Zakat is the third pillar of Islam, sitting between the prayer (salah) and the fast of Ramadan. In the Qur'an the command to establish prayer and give zakat is repeated many times as a single pairing — showing that worship of Allah and care for His creation are woven together. It is not an optional gift but a fixed, compulsory right that the poor hold over the wealth of the rich.

The word zakat means both purification and growth. Giving a small, fixed portion of your surplus purifies the rest of your wealth and your heart from greed, and — by Allah's promise — causes what remains to grow in blessing rather than shrink.

The standard rate on monetary wealth is one-fortieth, that is 2.5%. So for every 1,000 of qualifying wealth that has completed its lunar year above the threshold, 25 is due. This is a modest share by design: enough to circulate resources to those in need without straining the giver.

Zakat is not the same as sadaqah. Sadaqah is any voluntary charity, given in any amount, at any time, to almost anyone. Zakat is a defined obligation — a set rate, on set categories of wealth, once set conditions are met, paid to set categories of people. Neglecting it deliberately is a serious sin; both the Qur'an and Sunnah warn sternly against hoarding wealth while withholding its due.

purpose.title: Why zkt — purpose & wدیdom
purpose.summary: It purifies welth او  soul, او lifts  poیا
purpose.body:
Allah says of zakat: "Take from their wealth a charity by which you purify them and cause them to grow" (Qur'an 9:103). The obligation works on two levels at once — it purifies the giver's soul from stinginess and love of the world, and it purifies the wealth itself so that what stays in your hand is wholesome and blessed.

Socially, zakat is a divinely ordered system of circulation. When the Prophet ﷺ sent Mu'adh to Yemen he instructed that zakat be taken from their rich and given to their poor. Wealth is not meant to pile up among a few; zakat pulls it back into motion so the needy are fed, debtors are freed, and the community's bonds are strengthened.

Spiritually, giving zakat is an act of gratitude and trust. It answers the human urge to hoard with the certainty that provision comes from Allah, and it trains the believer to love giving. The one who pays zakat willingly finds their wealth protected, their heart lightened, and their reward stored with their Lord — "there will be no fear concerning them, nor will they grieve" (Qur'an 2:277).

zakatable.title: Wht دی generټولy zktble
zakatable.summary: Csh, metls, پهvestments, trde goods, receivbles
zakatable.body:
Zakat is due on wealth that has the potential to grow — money and things held as money — rather than on items you simply use. The main categories agreed upon across the schools are cash, gold and silver, trade goods, and (with their own rules) crops and livestock.

Commonly zakatable today: cash in hand and in bank accounts; gold and silver, including bullion, coins, and stored jewellery not in regular use; stocks, shares, and mutual funds valued at their current market price; the merchandise and inventory of a business (trade goods), valued at resale price; strong receivables — loans and invoices you reasonably expect to collect; and rental or business income you have saved rather than spent.

Many scholars also include accessible retirement savings and cryptocurrencies held as an asset, treating them like cash or investments. When in doubt, the guiding question is simple: is this wealth a store of value or a means of growth that I could liquidate? If so, it is likely zakatable. Value everything at today's market price on your zakat date — not at what you originally paid.

exempt.title: Wht دی usuټولy نه zktble
exempt.summary: Persپهl use items, wیاn jewellery, locked pensiپهs
exempt.body:
Wealth tied up in your ordinary daily life is generally not zakatable, because zakat targets growing wealth, not the things you live with and use. Your home, your car, your clothing, furniture, appliances, and the tools and equipment of your trade are all exempt — however valuable they are.

Gold and silver jewellery that a woman wears regularly is a well-known point of difference. The Hanafi school holds that all gold and silver is zakatable even if worn; the majority — Maliki, Shafi'i, and Hanbali — exempt jewellery kept for normal personal use but include it if it is hoarded as a store of wealth or exceeds customary adornment. Follow the ruling of the school you follow.

Pension or provident funds you cannot yet access are often excluded until the money actually comes into your hands, though some scholars require zakat on the accessible portion. Debts owed to you that are unlikely ever to be repaid are usually not counted until recovered. As always, the finer details vary between schools — when a case is unclear, ask a qualified scholar rather than guess.

debts.title: Debts & deductiپهs
debts.summary: Immedite debts my be deducted beلپارهe clcultپهg 2.5%
debts.body:
Zakat is calculated on your net zakatable wealth, so genuine debts you owe can reduce the amount on which you pay. The clearest case is debts due now — an unpaid personal loan, an outstanding credit-card balance, rent or bills already owed. Most scholars allow these to be subtracted from your gross wealth before you apply the 2.5%.

Long-term debts such as a mortgage or a multi-year instalment plan are handled with more care, because deducting the entire balance would wipe out the zakat of almost anyone with a home loan. A common contemporary approach is to deduct only the payments due within the coming year, not the whole outstanding sum. Schools and scholars differ here, so pick a consistent method under guidance.

Two cautions. First, do not treat future or hypothetical expenses as deductible debts — only what you actually owe counts. Second, do not subtract last year's unpaid zakat as if it were an ordinary debt; unpaid zakat remains a due obligation and should simply be paid. When your debt situation is complex, a scholar's ruling is worth more than a rough guess.

recipients.title: Who my receive zkt
recipients.body:
Zakat may only be given to the categories of people Allah Himself named in Surah at-Tawbah (9:60). This is one of the few acts of worship where the recipients are fixed by revelation, not left to the giver's preference. The eight categories are: the poor (al-fuqara); the needy (al-masakin); those employed to collect and administer zakat; those whose hearts are to be reconciled (al-mu'allafah); the freeing of captives and those in bondage (fi'r-riqab); the debt-burdened (al-gharimin); in the cause of Allah (fi sabil Allah); and the stranded traveller (ibn as-sabil).

It is not required to give to all eight; giving your zakat to even one eligible category fulfils the obligation, and directing it to the poor and needy is the most common practice.

Equally important is who may not receive it. Zakat cannot be given to the wealthy, nor to those you are already obliged to support — your parents, your children, or your spouse — since supporting them is a duty you owe anyway. In the classical view it is a personal transfer of ownership to an eligible individual, not a general donation; scholars differ on whether institutions such as masjids or broad public projects qualify under the cause of Allah. It also cannot be given to the family of the Prophet ﷺ, the Banu Hashim, as zakat. Aim it deliberately at people who match the Qur'anic categories.

otherRates.title: یا types د zkt & zkt l-fitr
otherRates.summary: Crops, livesتهck, او  pre-Eid zkt l-fitr differ
otherRates.body:
The 2.5% rate applies to money and trade wealth — zakat al-mal, which this calculator covers. Several other categories have entirely different rules and rates.

Crops and fruit have zakat due at harvest, not after a year: the rate is 10% (ushr) for land watered naturally by rain or springs, and 5% for land irrigated by artificial effort or cost. Grazing livestock — camels, cattle, sheep, and goats that graze freely for most of the year — have their own species-by-species nisab counts and sliding scales, drawn directly from the Sunnah.

Zakat al-fitr is different again, and every Muslim should know it. It is a small, fixed charity — about one sa' (roughly 2.5–3 kg) of a staple food such as dates, barley, wheat, or rice, or its cash value in many rulings — due at the end of Ramadan on behalf of every member of the household, young and old. Its purpose is to purify the fasting person from any shortfall and to ensure the poor also have food to celebrate Eid. The Prophet ﷺ commanded that it be paid before the Eid al-Fitr prayer; paid afterwards it counts only as ordinary charity. Each of these categories has its own detailed rulings — seek guidance specific to the asset.

mistakes.title: Commپه mدیtkes ته void
mistakes.summary: تېروتنهs هغه mke zkt پهvlid یا mدیclculted
mistakes.body:
Even sincere Muslims often slip on the practical details of zakat. Knowing the common errors helps you pay correctly and with peace of mind.

Forgetting the hawl or the anniversary: paying at a random time, or skipping years, leaves an outstanding obligation. Fix one Hijri date each year and assess your wealth on it.

Miscounting wealth: valuing gold or shares at their purchase price instead of today's market value, forgetting cash held in multiple accounts or currencies, or overlooking business inventory and money owed to you. Zakat is on everything zakatable that you own on your date.

Giving to the wrong people: handing zakat to parents, children, or a spouse you already support, or treating it as a generic donation to any good cause. It must reach one of the eight Qur'anic categories.

Intention errors: giving generously all year but never intending any of it as zakat. Zakat is an act of worship and needs the intention (niyyah) that this particular payment is your obligatory zakat.

Over-deducting debts: subtracting a whole long-term mortgage, or future expenses that are not yet owed, to shrink the bill. Only real, current liabilities reduce your zakatable wealth. When any of these is unclear for your situation, ask a qualified scholar rather than assume.
